description.narrative: Food assistance to 1,200 vulnerable households, some 8,400 people, including the vulnerability assessment, the procurement and distribution of food parcels and post-distribution monitoring. Support to three YRCS primary health centres in Sa'dah, Sana'a Governorate and Ad Dhali', covering essential operational costs, the procurement of medicines and medical supplies and the strengthening of the referral system to higher-level hospitals, including ambulance costs, reaching approximately 36,000 people. Rehabilitation and upgrading of a strategic water supply system using climate-resilient and energy-efficient solutions, the establishment and training of community water committees and water quality monitoring at three sources, benefiting 15,000 people.
Members of vulnerable communities affected by conflict in Yemen

The project runs for twelve months, from 1 July 2026 to 30 June 2027, and covers selected districts in Marib, Raymah, Sa'dah, Sana'a Governorate and Ad Dhali'. It combines food security, health and WASH interventions and is expected to reach 59,400 people in total. The locations were prioritised against the UNOCHA HNRP 2026, the JIAF 2026 severity analysis, the IPC results of May and June 2026, flood exposure, IDP presence and operational feasibility, with most classified at intersectoral severity level 4.

fter nearly a decade of conflict, Yemen remains one of the most severe protracted crises in the world. The de facto truce has held since 2022, but the conflict is unresolved and the structural drivers of vulnerability, economic collapse and weakened public institutions, continue to deepen needs. The HNRP 2026 estimates that 22.3 million people, more than half the population, require humanitarian assistance and protection, including 5.2 million internally displaced. The health system is critically strained: only around 59 percent of facilities are fully functional, 19.3 million people need health assistance, immunisation coverage stands at roughly 63 percent and falls below 45 percent in hard-to-reach and frontline-adjacent districts, and cholera, measles and dengue remain endemic threats. Access is itself a determinant of mortality, with 70 percent of the rural population living more than thirty minutes from a functional emergency obstetric care centre. On the WASH side, 14.4 million people are in need, and the degradation of the Al Hodeidah and Aden networks carries a constant risk of explosive cholera transmission during the rainy seasons.
Food insecurity compounds this picture. The IPC analysis of May and June 2026 places close to five million people in Government of Yemen controlled areas at Phase 3 or above, including some 1.4 million at Phase 4, and projects 5.4 million at Phase 3 or above during the June to September lean season, with 1.6 million at Phase 4. Levels are expected to remain critically high through the October to December harvest period, which indicates that seasonal production cannot offset conflict, currency depreciation and reduced humanitarian assistance. Since April 2026, heavy rains and flooding have added a further shock, affecting 83,713 people across 254 recorded incidents, with 30 deaths and 47 injuries, and destroying homes, roads, water systems and livelihoods. All of this unfolds against a severe response deficit: as of 17 June 2026 the HNRP was only 14.8 percent funded, up from 12.2 percent in April, which has forced the humanitarian community to target only 9.4 million of the people with the most acute needs.
